title: Grief in the texts
hookLine: the Buddha's attendant leans on a door frame and weeps, and the texts keep it in
tomorrow: so the tears are allowed. then what do you do with them?

cards: At some funerals, people say it as praise: she was so strong, she didn't cry once. So was Ananda wrong? He was the Buddha's attendant for years, the one at his side.
Near the end, at a place called Kusinara, Ananda slips into a building, leans against the door frame, and weeps.
I'm still a learner, he says, with so much left to do, and my teacher, who was so kind to me, is about to pass away. The old texts could have left that scene out, or tidied it up. They didn't.

teach.b: The Buddha asks where Ananda is, hears he's weeping, and sends for him. What he says next has been read two ways inside the tradition, and both readings have the text on their side.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: CALM IS THE AIM.
teach.b: The first view: calm is the aim. The Buddha tells Ananda, enough, don't grieve, don't lament; haven't I taught that we're parted from all that is dear?
And when the Buddha dies, the same sutta says some monks wept and fell to the ground, while those free of passion bore it mindfully, saying: things are impermanent, how could it be otherwise?
On this view, the tears are honest, and the path points beyond them. The second view: look at what the Buddha does before and after those words. He sends for Ananda instead of leaving him alone.

Then he praises him, for years of kindness in deed, in word and in thought, and tells him he'll soon be free too. Nobody shames him. The texts keep his tears in plain sight, next to the teacher's tenderness.
On this view, grief is part of being human on the path, and it's met with warmth before it's met with teaching.

teach.h: NO ONE LEFT ALONE AT THE DOOR.
teach.b: Notice the two views share something.
Neither one hides the tears, and neither one leaves Ananda crying alone at the door.

how: At Buddhist funerals, practice varies: some communities keep a calm, chanting atmosphere and others make room for open weeping; teachers often retell Ananda at Kusinara when people ask whether grief is allowed.

games.q: what does “grief in the texts” mean?
o: the ancient debate over whether the Buddha himself cried
how the old sutta texts show sorrow, tears and all, with care
a list of rules in the texts about how long to mourn

games.q: what happened at Kusinara — tap the pairs.
p: leaned on the door frame and wept
sent for him and praised his kindness
calm is the aim; tears point beyond
warmth comes first; grief is human

s: the early texts leave out Ananda's tears to keep him looking calm
they keep them in plain sight: Ananda weeping at the door frame.
the Buddha praised Ananda for kindness in deed, word and thought
after sending for him, he praised years of loving service.
in the sutta, the Buddha also tells Ananda not to grieve
he says enough, don't lament; we're parted from all that is dear. that's why view one has the text on its side too.

games.q: your friend says a real Buddhist wouldn't cry at a funeral. you disagree, but she asks for her side's best case from the text. what is it?
o: Buddhists think crying is rude to the family at a funeral.
the Buddha told Ananda enough, don't lament, and the freed monks bore the death calmly.
the texts never mention anyone crying, so calm must be the rule.
games.why: that's the strongest case for view one, and it's in the sutta. view two answers from the same pages: he sent for Ananda, praised him, and nobody shamed his tears.

practice: Sit up, and rest one hand flat on your chest. Let your shoulders drop and your jaw loosen. If something sad is near, let it come up as far as it wants to, without pushing it out or pulling it in.
Your hand stays there the whole time, the way a teacher sends for a friend.

wordCard.voice: Grief in the texts: Ananda weeping at the door frame, a teacher who sends for him, and two honest readings of what came next.

orig.note: Pali: Ananda, the Buddha's attendant; as a word, ananda means joy.

carryVoice: Pocket line: even Ananda wept, and whichever reading you lean toward, he wasn't left alone. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta, ch. 5 (Ananda weeps leaning on the door frame; the Buddha sends for him, says 'enough, Ananda', and praises his service in deed, word and thought)
Digha Nikaya 16, ch. 6 (at the passing, some monks weep while those free of passion bear it mindfully: 'impermanent are formations')
